papers.title: Why We Created Yet Another Memory Framework: Understanding MGA's Role in Next-Gen Database Systems

papers.abstract: Despite the presence of multiple memory regions in modern database systems, supporting an efficient form of memory remains a challenge under production constraints. In enterprise-grade data systems, existing abstractions impose a trade-off between coarsegrained global sharing and strict process isolation, resulting in data copying, memory fragmentation, and limited support for controlled sharing. These challenges become more pronounced as workloads grow more diverse, and systems must tolerate process failures while maintaining predictable performance. This paper introduces the Managed Global Area (MGA), a scoped shared-memory abstraction in Oracle AI Database that addresses these limitations. MGA allows components to explicitly define allocation source, membership, and coordination semantics across selected processes while integrating with a production database engine. Unlike fully shared memory regions in Oracle, such as the System Global Area (SGA), MGA supports dynamic process membership and modular memory usage without imposing system-wide visibility. We evaluate MGA on analytical and AI workloads that stress shared-memory execution, including TPC-H hash joins and ONNX Runtime inference. Under concurrent execution, MGA reduces latency for join-intensive TPC-H queries by up to 35%. For ONNX-based inference, MGA-enabled model sharing reduces memory footprint by up to 90% and lowers large-model inference latency by up to 37%. These results demonstrate that dynamically scoped shared memory can improve both efficiency and predictability in production database systems.

papers.title: OceanBase Bacchus: A High-Performance and Scalable Cloud-Native Shared Storage Architecture for Multi-Cloud
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，带生产环境信号，涉及解耦式架构
papers.abstract: Although more databases embrace shared-storage architectures, current storage-disaggregated systems lack an optimal balance between cost and performance. B+-tree-based shared storage struggles with frequent in-place updates under high concurrency; disaggregated designs still require a scalable shared-log path for multi-writer OLTP. This paper presents OceanBase Bacchus, a production-grade disaggregated shared-storage architecture for OceanBase. We foreground two technical elements: (i) service-oriented PALF logging with sharded log streams and multiple Read-Write (RW) leaders, where partition-local ordering is composed with distributed 2PC across stream leaders , breaking the single-writer bottleneck of classic shared-log designs while preserving ACID, and (ii) a Shared Block Cache Service that pools macro-blocks within an availability zone, a less common alternative to purely per-node caches and motivated by stateless compute scaling. Cloud object storage backs the LSM-tree capacity tier for cost, but we do not treat "LSM + object storage" as the headline novelty (precedents exist). Bacchus's value is integrating and hardening these mechanisms in a shipping system, demonstrated by credible OLTP/OLAP performance and substantial storage-cost reductions. The architecture decouples modules and enables elastic scaling of compute, cache, and storage independently. Experimental results show that Ocean-Base Bacchus matches or exceeds HBase and PolarDB in OLTP and significantly outperforms StarRocks in OLAP. With multi-cloud support, the system retains high availability and competitive performance while cutting storage costs by 59% (OLTP) and 89% (OLAP).

papers.abstract: As server CPUs scale to dozens and now hundreds of cores per socket, parallel query engines must rethink how they redistribute data between threads. Partitioned operators such as hash joins and aggregations require frequent data redistribution across threads, yet existing intra-process shuffle designs fundamentally fail to scale with core count: batch partitioning avoids cross-thread synchronization in the hot path but materializes all intermediate data, introduces a global producer/consumer barrier, and requires a consumption approach with low cache locality, while channel-based streaming avoids materialization but incurs per-channel synchronization that scales poorly with core count. As core counts rise, these architectural tradeoffs increasingly prevent engines from fully utilizing modern hardware. We present a ring-buffer streaming shuffle design that addresses these shortcomings through lock-free atomic slot acquisition into fixed-size batch groups, achieving amortized O (1) synchronization cost per batch and O ( M ) memory independent of input size. Ring-buffer shuffle has been implemented in Redpanda's Oxla query engine for two years, where it currently powers production queries for Redpanda SQL users. We evaluate all three approaches on a 72-core NVIDIA Grace-Hopper, a 192-core dual-socket AWS Graviton4, and a 96-core (192-thread) AMD EPYC. On a 72-core single-socket system the ring buffer outperforms channel streaming by up to 44% and batch partitioning by up to 79%; at 192 cores the advantage over channel grows to over 100% and over 300% versus batch partitioning. Even so, on chiplet architectures with many partitioned L3 caches, the shared atomic counter becomes a cross-die bottleneck and channel-based streaming remains competitive. End-to-end Graviton4 evaluation on TPC-H (21 queries) and ClickBench (43 queries) shows the advantage is workload-shape-dependent: the ring buffer wins TPC-H in aggregate (1.07×) across diverse query shapes, but a handful of consumer-heavy patterns—COUNT(DISTINCT), wide aggregates—favor channels and swing ClickBench's aggregate the other way.

To break this impasse, we propose ScaleSense, a proactive, query-level resource scaling framework. Specifically, it features a multi-faceted query encoder that jointly models plan topologies and hardware specifications. Crucially, a quantile-based resource predictor estimates multi-dimensional physical footprints, acting as a reliable safety net for optimal resource scaling. An auto-scaling controller then navigates the performance-cost Pareto frontier, dynamically tailoring allocations to specific business priorities without requiring model retraining. Evaluations on over 1.36 million production queries show that ScaleSense achieves state-of-the-art prediction accuracy with good prediction interval coverage. papers.title: E-LQO: A Comprehensive Energy Evaluation Framework for Learned Query Optimization
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，带基准测试，有实验评估，关注延迟
papers.abstract: Learned Query Optimization (LQO) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving database performance, with reported speedups of 2× to over 10× on standard benchmarks. Existing evaluations, however, remain largely latency-centric and leave the energy debt from data collection, model training, and online inference less visible. This paper presents E-LQO, the first comprehensive framework for evaluating energy consumption across the complete LQO lifecycle: data collection or preparation, model training, model inference, and plan execution. We formalize two domain-specific metrics— Energy Return on Investment (EROI) and Energy Payback Time (EPT)—to quantify both per-cycle efficiency and the amortization horizon of learned optimizers. Across seven LQO methods on fixed-scale JOB and on TPC-H/TPC-DS up to 100 GB, we find that lifecycle energy is governed less by whether an optimizer is learned than by how it obtains supervision. Execution-based systems buy plan quality through active exploration and carry a large upfront energy debt; passive/log-driven systems can repay much faster with reusable logs or labels, but this advantage depends on incremental-cost accounting and often comes with weaker latency gains on light workloads. We further show that total online inference energy, including candidate-plan generation, enables symmetric accounting, and that roughly 50% template coverage is the energy-optimal exploration region for the execution-based methods we study. E-LQO provides practitioners with actionable guidance for energy-conscious deployment decisions and exposes optimization opportunities for sustainable learned query optimization.

papers.abstract: Modern cloud platforms provide diverse compute services, including virtual machines, Function-as-a-Service, and Query-as-a-Service, each offering unique trade-offs in performance, elasticity, and cost. While these services collectively cover the diverse needs of OLAP workloads, existing systems typically rely on a single service type or static rule-based scheduling. However, no single service is optimal for dynamic OLAP workloads with diverse performance characteristics and resource requirements. Consequently, efficient query execution requires scheduling workloads across heterogeneous services, which introduces three challenges. (1) Heterogeneous service models. Distinct billing models and execution paradigms (e.g., stateful or stateless) complicate the comparison of services. (2) Scheduling complexity at scale. High query concurrency exacerbates resource contention, creating a vast search space that makes identifying optimal scheduling decisions in real time computationally expensive. (3) Unpredictable runtime dynamics. Cloud infrastructure exhibits performance fluctuations due to factors like multi-tenant interference and scaling delays, which can invalidate initial scheduling decisions and cause suboptimal performance. In this paper, we present EASE, a resource-aware query scheduling framework designed to orchestrate OLAP queries across heterogeneous cloud compute services. EASE addresses these challenges through three integrated mechanisms. First, EASE incorporates a heterogeneity-aware cost model that captures distinct service characteristics to guide service selection. Second, EASE employs a real-time query scheduler that resolves resource contention under high concurrency. Third, EASE implements a dynamic rescheduler that mitigates runtime fluctuations by proactively migrating queries subject to unexpected delays. Our evaluation demonstrates that EASE significantly improves query performance and cost efficiency, reducing query latency by up to 35% and monetary cost by up to 67% compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

We study HNSW hyperparameter tuning from a systems perspective and show that its configuration space exhibits strong structural regularities. Across multiple datasets and HNSW-based vector search engines, CHAT identifies configurations that maximize recall or throughput while satisfying constraints on accuracy, latency, build time, index size, and tuning budget. We also discuss the current limitations of GenDB, such as high generation cost and the lack of correctness guarantees, to inform future extensions. papers.title: Future-Proof Data Systems

papers.abstract: Database systems are increasingly expected to support evolution in data workloads, representations, and hardware environments. Existing designs often respond through either specialization, which can deliver high performance but leads to narrow and brittle systems, or extensibility, which broadens functionality but can produce opaque extensions and growing system complexity. This paper summarizes a line of work that treats future-proofness as an abstraction-design problem: we identify boundaries across the data processing stack where concerns must evolve independently, and design interfaces that preserve enough structure across that boundary for optimization. We illustrate this at three levels of the stack. At the level of data structures, Sortledton unifies analytics, pattern matching, and transactional updates on a single graph representation. At the level of data formats, AnyBlox allows engines to read datasets that provide sandboxed self-decoding logic, reducing the need for bespoke readers. At the level of query processing, LingoDB and its declarative sub-operator layer recast query optimization as a sequence of extensible compiler passes, enabling cross-domain optimization and hardware-specific lowerings.

Evaluation on HATtrick shows that HeraDB outperforms Colibri in maximum individual TP/AP throughput, achieving up to 11.1× higher TP and 5.9× higher AP with high data freshness and strong performance isolation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become pivotal for enhancing the capabilities of modern large models. Existing systems fail to address these two concerns in a unified manner. Techniques that tightly control data staleness often constrain effective data skewness mitigation, while aggressive data skewness mitigation tends to exacerbate data staleness. As a result, systems are forced to trade off convergence for performance, or vice versa. To address this, we propose StaleFlow, an RL post-training system that jointly tackles data staleness and skewness. First, to control staleness, StaleFlow introduces a global consistency protocol that tracks the full lifecycle of each trajectory and constrains staleness. Second, to mitigate skewness, StaleFlow re-designs the RL system architecture by constructing data servers for trajectories and parameters to achieve flexible rollout coordination. Subsequently, we develop a suite of staleness-aware, throughput-oriented strategies to enhance system performance. Evaluations show that StaleFlow achieves up to 1.42-2.68× (1.18-1.91× on average) higher throughput than state-of-the-art systems, without compromising convergence. Taking full advantage of TPU slices and JAX distributed computing, we seamlessly scale our execution environment to run TPC-H benchmark up to Scale Factor 1000 (SF1000). The results establish TPUs not merely as dense neural compute hardware, but as a highly competitive, massively scalable substrate for the next generation of analytical query processing.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce Real-Time SPM in Oracle 26ai, a novel extension of SPM that performs foreground verification of new execution plans during user query execution. Hence, we propose ALORE, a scalable and domain-robust overlap ratio estimator built on three principles: (P1) explicitly represent row-column structure; (P2) expose inter-table alignment signals during training without expensive alignment search; (P3) reduce sensitivity to corpus-specific value distributions. ALORE instantiates these principles with a Two-View Row-Column Hypergraph encoder, alignment-guided objectives with inexpensive interaction signals, and a domain-robust value mapping. Experiments on datasets spanning diverse domains and scales, including a large real-world corpus beyond prior benchmarks, show that ALORE outperforms the state of the art. ALORE reduces MAE by up to 55% overall and 69% in zero-shot transfer, while achieving up to 89x speedup. We further validate its effectiveness for query-by-table retrieval.

KLL-Polymer inherits the idea of hierarchical sampling from the KLL sketch, but aggregates items by key during the sampling process, thus enabling a single sketch to efficiently handle multiple keys, rather than maintaining separate KLL sketches for each key. We further introduce a deterministic-compaction variant of KLL-Polymer, which optimizes its performance by more effectively filtering infrequent keys at the top levels. papers.abstract: Resistance distance computation is a fundamental problem in graph data management. To avoid the high latency of online evaluation, recent work builds offline indexes. Existing approaches, however, fall into two families with complementary weaknesses: loop-erased random-walk methods (e.g., LEIndex) are efficient on fast-mixing graphs but suffer high variance on sparse or tree-like topologies, whereas Cholesky-based methods (e.g., TreeIndex) perform well on small-treewidth graphs but are costly to construct for large, dense networks. Building on this insight, we present Tree+DAG, an index that unifies deterministic matrix decomposition with loop-erased random walk sampling. We first apply a core–tree decomposition to split the graph into a tree-like periphery and a dense core. The periphery is isolated via TreeIndex—a compact hierarchical tree labelling that exploits the nonzero pattern of the Cholesky factors of the inverse Laplacian. papers.abstract: Distributed transactional consistency over partitions is costly: classical two-phase commit (2PC) incurs high coordination and latency, and dynamic partition transfers complicate recovery. We introduce a tree-structured 2PC framework for OceanBase (OB) using single-machine log streams in three ways. First, we use log streams as coalesced 2PC participants: co-located partitions that would each be separate in a partition-centric design share one log-stream participant, so a transaction spanning N such partitions interacts with one participant in commit, cutting coordination by orders of magnitude (e.g., 99% for N = 100). Second, a coordinator-rooted DAG recursively builds commit trees; migration contexts as leaves avoid explicit participant-list updates and circular dependencies while ensuring linearizable commits under topology change. Third, prepare_unknown and trans_unknown states prevent violations when participants lose context; they signal uncertainty during retries, avoiding erroneous aborts from "lying" participants while isolating users from ambiguity. Experiments approach single-machine transaction performance with lower latency and bandwidth consumption, supporting modern distributed databases.

papers.title: CADENZA in Action: Breaking the Monolith with Intent-Dependent Plan Spaces for Semantic Queries
papers.importance_reason: 关注延迟
papers.abstract: Semantic query processing engines execute semantic operators, whose behavior is specified by natural-language intents, via model inference over multimodal data. Most existing optimizers optimize the operators at the granularity of monolithic implementations—such as LLMs and embedding models—forcing a trade-off between expensive model calls and cheaper alternatives that fail to capture intent-dependent semantics. We present CADENZA, a semantic operator optimizer that compiles an intent into decomposed steps, selects concrete physical implementations for each step, and tunes their parameters under user-specified quality-latency-cost preferences. In this demonstration, users interact with CADENZA through a web interface over multimodal databases, exploring how an intent is decomposed into alternative plans, how each plan is optimized, and how different preferences yield different winning plans.

papers.title: GraphAlg Playground: An Online Platform for Learning and Experimenting with the GraphAlg Language

papers.abstract: The GraphAlg language for graph algorithms enables native support for user-defined graph analytics workloads in databases. In this demonstration, we present a web-based playground for writing and executing GraphAlg programs in the web browser, including an interactive tutorial explaining its key concepts. The playground runs inside the user's web browser without any installation, and is freely available under a permissive license as a reusable library. We present two demonstration scenarios of the publicly available playground website, showing how new users can learn to program in GraphAlg using the tutorial, while expert users can use the playground to prototype and validate their algorithms.

papers.abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly rely on external data to complete downstream tasks such as model training and decision support. However, existing data discovery systems remain largely retrieval-oriented: they surface candidate datasets from heterogeneous sources, but provide limited support for estimating task-specific utility, selecting cost-effective datasets under budget constraints, or incorporating trustworthy feedback from prior usage. This paper presents Guixu, a valuation-driven data discovery system for autonomous agents. Guixu employs a three-phase valuation pipeline with proxy-label propagation and multi-round knapsack optimization for task-aware data valuation. Guixu integrates agentic payment protocol to enable budget-constrained data procurement workflows. Guixu leverages on-chain data market and attestation signals for verifiable data discovery. Our demonstration highlights how Guixu enables an agent to move beyond keyword-based dataset retrieval toward task- and budget-aware, trustworthy data discovery and procurement. Attendees can interactively explore the full workflow, from NL task specification and multi-source search to data valuation and verifiable transaction feedback.

papers.title: Hermes at Scale: Powering Distributed Queries with a Unified Memory Fabric

papers.abstract: MySQL is a widely used database management system. However, it has clear deficits for analytical workloads. To improve analytical performance, we introduced Hermes as an accelerator for MySQL. Since many workloads easily fit a single node/machine, we originally developed Hermes for this case. However, Hermes on a single node has a major limitation: Storage space is limited to a single-node, even worse, to main memory of a single node. In this paper, we address this problem by making Hermes distributed. New nodes can be added that bring additional resources, i.e. memory and compute, to the cluster. Hermes' storage can automatically expand to the new nodes. Our design operates as logically "Shared Memory" via an abstraction layer (Memcom). We argue that modern interconnects make shared memory feasible without extreme performance penalties. To further minimize sending data over the network, we annotate larger data blocks with localities, which allows reader nodes to locate and read local data. In addition, we extended Hermes' query execution to multiple nodes as well. This is implemented via a new Planner that splits the query plan into tasks and defines how query execution is parallelized (MPP intra-query parallelism). Each task is separated via data sharing operators (Portals) that write intermediates to a shared memory pool (Memcom). We extended scans to pick up row groups (our granularity of data storage) based on their locality. Therefore, distributed scans will preferably read local data (thanks to our predefined localities) and only when there is no more local data to be read consider remote data. We experimentally show that our approach is not only competitive in terms of performance but outperforms well-known open-source systems by more than 11×. Compared to industrial-grade cloud systems, Hermes also outperforms by 1.5×.

papers.abstract: GaussDB is Huawei's premier database system, designed for large-scale deployments and the most demanding workloads. It is a distributed shared-nothing system, capable of handling all types of workloads. This paper outlines a series of modifications to GaussDB aimed at improving its performance on large-scale and complex analytical workloads. After these changes, its performance on the TPC-H workload exceeded the best published result by 40% at 30 TB. The key enhancements to achieve this elite performance include adopting a pipeline execution model, a faster and more scalable inter-node data shuffle, exploiting a unified bus and unified remote memory access. We also expanded the support of cost-based Bloom filter placement and implemented several Bloom filter streaming strategies, enabling their use across nodes.

papers.title: The Case for Single-Version Concurrency Control in the Cloud
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) has been the dominant concurrency protocol in modern database management systems (DBMSs). However, cloud-native HTAP architectures shift many of MVCC's traditional advantages from the primary transaction engine to the deployment architecture. Now, transactional and analytical processing are decoupled into loosely synchronized engines, while cloud deployment primitives provide the workload isolation required for this design. In this paper, we challenge the status quo, arguing that single-version concurrency control (SVCC) is better suited to cloud transaction processing than MVCC. Through a systematic analysis of MVCC's limitations, we show that SVCC avoids these shortcomings through a more lightweight and efficient design. Beyond arguing for a lighter transaction processing, we use this SVCC effort as a blueprint to advocate for a broader rethinking of cloud-native architectures and to outline a research roadmap to shape next-generation DBMSs.

papers.title: JetStream: Generating Verified Query Accelerators for Existing Database Systems

papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that LLMs can synthesize highly specialized database systems for fixed workloads, but these systems replace the DBMS's native storage and assume static data: users must migrate their data, often give up ad-hoc queries, and lose acceleration once the data changes. We present JetStream, which instead generates query-specific accelerators that extend an existing DBMS. Given a set of parametrized query templates, a staged agentic workflow synthesizes accelerators that run directly over the DBMS's native tables and may maintain custom auxiliary state, while the DBMS remains responsible for storage, transactions, recovery, and all other queries. A fixed, engine-neutral substrate handles engine-specific hooks and keeps auxiliary state transactionally consistent under writes. JetStream generates two kinds of accelerators: tested accelerators, which may use any optimization and are validated by differential testing, and verified accelerators which trade some performance for a machine-checked proof that every answer satisfies a trusted specification derived from the SQL. On TPC-H at SF=20, JetStream achieves a $315 \times$ geomean read speedup over DuckDB ($93 \times$ verified) and retains $120 \times$ under a continuous update stream of 10,000 modified rows per second.

papers.title: ConStore: Search-Overlapped Prefetch and Co-Retrieval-Aware Content Storage for Disk-Based ANNS

papers.abstract: Disk-based approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) supports retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), search, recommendation, and advertising over corpora that exceed memory capacity. Existing ANNS research often focuses on vector search at small top-K, whereas industrial-scale applications require larger retrieval sets. Fetching the corresponding content from storage remains comparatively underexplored. Our profiling across million- to billion-vector corpora shows that, at large K, content fetch latency can match or exceed vector-search latency and cannot be ignored in end-to-end retrieval. We present ConStore, a content storage engine combining two complementary techniques to reduce end-to-end retrieval latency. Speculative Inline Content Prefetch (SICP) commonly abstracts graph-based and cluster-based ANNS as progressive SSD I/O that refines an in-flight candidate queue. It prefetches content for stable leading candidates under a bounded I/O budget, overlapping content reads with search without changing the final top-K results. Co-Retrieval-Pattern-Aware Grouping (RPAG) uses query logs to place frequently co-retrieved documents in contiguous segments. Workload-Adaptive Segment Reorganization (WASR) adapts this layout to workload shifts by selectively regrouping segments under a bounded rewrite budget. Group Content Fetch (GCF) exploits this layout to coalesce per-document random reads into batched, page-aware I/O requests. SICP works independently of the content layout, while RPAG and GCF reduce fetch cost even without prefetching. Across three multi-hop QA workloads with K from 10 to 1600, ConStore reduces end-to-end retrieval latency over the best per-document-read baseline by up to 48% on DiskANN and 25% on SPANN. Separate experiments on 100M- and billion-vector indexes demonstrate SICP's applicability at larger scales.

papers.title: Reflective Compositional Grounding for Natural-Language-to-SPARQL

papers.abstract: Natural-language query generation over large knowledge graphs embodies the classical vocabulary problem in human-systems communication. We present an NL2SPARQL framework that places conceptual compositionality at the center of query interpretation and connects it to the relational composition required for binding and query construction. A fixed concept encoder represents compound expressions jointly, and schema candidates are ranked using semantic similarity, type compatibility, and hierarchy proximity. Reflective refinement critically examines how the grounded meanings are realized through argument bindings, joins, and operator scope. Diagnosed semantic discrepancies guide revisions to the responsible stage. We formalise a monotone refinement discipline that accumulates scoped interpretation requirements and establish conditions under which changes to the composed process preserve previously validated interpretations. Across five benchmark/knowledge-graph targets, mean schema recall@10 increases from 0.712 to 0.837. With retrieval held fixed, reflective prompt rewriting adds 2.27-3.33 answer-F1 points. These experiments evaluate the grounding and refinement mechanisms, while the formal analysis specifies the stronger requirements for conservative adaptation across queries.

papers.title: Building SQL Equivalence Proofs from Query Rewrite Rules

papers.abstract: Query rewriting and semantic evaluation of text-to-SQL systems both depend on deciding whether two SQL queries return the same result on every database satisfying the schema constraints. Building on this observation, \sys{} organizes query-rewriting knowledge as a standalone proof-producing system. It separates rule validation from proof discovery, explicitly aligns alternative query representations, and returns the resulting rewrite derivation. Across three corpus classes, EquiTrace proves 648/1,106 expected-equivalent text-to-SQL pairs (58.6%), 229/266 curated pairs (86.1%), and 97/240 LLM-generated rewrites whose results agree under benchmark execution (40.4%). On the query rewrite corpus, EquiTrace proves 97 pairs, compared with 35 for QED and 38 for SQLSolver. An analysis of 1,242 recorded proofs shows that coverage depends on a small number of transformations, while many frequently used rules are individually substitutable. The resulting derivations make each proof replayable and expose the specific transformations on which it depends.

papers.title: Conflicted Records: Typed Adversarial Contracts for Auditable LLM Output Quality Enforcement

The question is whether a deterministic check over structured inter-agent records can catch the defects that referential checks alone miss. We present BiasGuard-D: two adversarial roles drawn from distinct model families exchange typed claim documents, a three-model quorum adjudicates by majority vote, and a combined referential-plus-semantic invariant validates the verdict. The semantic component fires on verdicts referential checks miss; removing the iterative loop drops invariant satisfaction sharply. The deliberation layer transfers from stereotype to hallucination remediation on HaluEval QA with only role-framing changes, raising right-answer recovery by 49 percentage points; the triage gate required a cross-family second auditor to maintain recall on objective hallucination. Every claim, vote, and instruction is stored as a typed record giving operators a provenance trail auditable under emerging AI regulations.

papers.abstract: Existing approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) methods generally assume that each entity has a single vector. To address these issues, we propose ACTIVE, a dynamic Pareto-frontier-based DVQ index that supports efficient construction and updates while maintaining high retrieval performance under varying query preferences. It employs angle-constrained active-range computation and connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair strategies to accelerate node insertion and deletion, respectively. Extensive experiments show that, at comparable (or slightly below) search accuracy, ACTIVE improves insertion throughput by $1.20$--$1.43\times$ over DEG, and deletion throughput by $1.64$--$2.06\times$ over neighbor-reconnection-based repair and by $22.64$--$39.51\times$ over reinsertion-based repair.

papers.title: Taming Multi-Dimensional Skew in Sparse Matrix Multiplication with Contention-Aware Scheduling [Technical Report]

papers.abstract: Sparse general matrix-matrix multiplication (SpGEMM) is a key kernel in graph analytics, relational queries, and machine learning. Yet, its performance remains a significant challenge, due to the inherent sparsity and, more critically, the prevalent skew patterns often found in real-world workloads. This paper investigates this problem and demonstrates that an unbalanced workload distribution is the main culprit, harming performance through two co-existing root causes: first, multi-dimensional skew, where imbalance across computation cost, output density, and data locality cannot be captured by any single balancing metric; and second, cache contention, where dense substructures induce severe on-chip interference. To that end, we propose adaptive morsel scheduling (AMS), a dynamic scheduling framework that decouples skew dimensions via fixed-result-size morsels and integrates contention-aware load balancing (CALB) and data-conscious simultaneous multithreading activator (SMTact) to alleviate cache-level contention, alongside a hybrid accumulation mechanism (HYB) that adaptively selects the best accumulator per morsel. Evaluations across matrix squaring, relational queries, graph analytics, and other sparse matrix kernels show that AMS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on skewed workloads while maintaining comparable performance on non-skewed ones. These gains, along with improved bandwidth utilization, remain valid across a wide range of workloads and hardware systems.

papers.title: G-CasDec: General Cascaded Decompression on GPUs

Also, none of them provides an extensible way to easily add new schemes. To address these issues, we present G-CasDec, an optimized framework to enable efficient decompression on GPUs for general cascaded compression schemes. G-CasDec incorporates several key techniques, including aligned batching for aggressive compression of variable-length data yet with efficient decompression, shared memory reuse and register-level fusion to improve resource utilization, and a set of bytecode instructions to orchestrate a generic decompression flow. G-CasDec outperforms state-of-the-art designs with 2.8× higher compression ratios and 2.0× faster decompression, and is also extensible to arbitrary cascade schemes.

Private ANNS (PANNS) allows a client to retrieve nearest neighbors without revealing its query. The state-of-the-art single-server scheme, Pacmann (ICLR'25), achieves high accuracy via graph-based search with private information retrieval (PIR), but incurs substantial communication overhead because each PIR query retrieves only a single vertex. We present Amora, a communication-efficient PANNS system that applies SimplePIR to a partitioned graph index so that one PIR query is amortized over many vertices. To retrieve as much of the distance and neighbor information the search needs under a limited communication budget, Amora adopts a dual-PIR split layout with two heterogeneous PIR matrices that stay balanced in dimension: VecPIR retrieves inner products for an entire partition of vertices as their distance at once, while NbrPIR retrieves necessary neighbor lists at subgroup granularity for graph traversal. This layout shifts the cost model of PIR query from per-vertex to per-partition, which significantly reduces the communication overhead. To further improve efficiency by reducing the number of scans and query rounds in the PIR database, Amora introduces batch PIR to pack multiple queries into one matrix multiplication, centroid-based pruning to filter unpromising partitions, and TopCand exploration that seeds jump-style graph navigation with the closest vertices from each retrieved partition. We evaluate Amora on five datasets spanning 96 to 1024 dimensions and up to 10 million vectors. Compared to Pacmann, Amora reduces online communication by 93--99% while achieving higher search accuracy.

papers.title: WaRP: Workload-Aware Request Planning for Vector Retrieval on Object Storage

papers.abstract: Modern vector search systems keep payload vectors in cloud object storage and only a compact routing index on fast local storage, typically using cluster-based ANN indexes. Existing readers either issue one request per probed cluster, or coalesce adjacent ranges with hand-tuned gap or span thresholds that do not transfer across datasets or query workloads. We formulate the grouping of probed-cluster byte intervals into object-store requests as a global per-query optimization problem and present WaRP, a workload-aware request planner that solves it efficiently. Given the sorted byte intervals, a limit on the number of requests per query, and an estimate of how many object-store requests from one query can proceed concurrently under the target serving configuration, WaRP searches for a merge plan that minimizes a concurrency-aware latency surrogate while satisfying the request limit. Using an optimized dynamic program and adaptive frontier search, WaRP returns a plan within $(1{+}ε)$ of the optimum, with per-query planning overhead under $10$ms even in the most demanding tested settings. A lightweight offline reordering pass further improves request mergeability without changing the semantics of ANN search. We implement WaRP inside Lance's I/O scheduler and evaluate it on AWS S3. We build IVFPQ indexes on seven datasets, including SIFT100M and DEEP100M at the 100M-vector scale. WaRP + Reorder improves QPS by $1.09--3.48\times$ and reduces GETs by $2.12--5.19\times$ relative to Lance, while preserving Lance's recall.

The LLM is used only during offline rule discovery. At inference time, prediction is a transparent key lookup with no model-serving requirement. Experiments on enterprise sales-order prediction and public relational benchmarks show that cascades are most effective when fields follow stable business rules, while learned graph models remain preferable when prediction depends on temporal or neighborhood patterns. papers.title: When the Application Layer Is Disposable: Putting Integrity Constraints Back in the Database

However, beyond keys, single-row CHECKs, and referential integrity, most constraints are enforced by application layers today. SQL ASSERTIONs, standardized in SQL-92, remain poorly supported by major RDBMSs. This has become increasingly unacceptable due to two developments. First, LLM-driven applications and agents increasingly issue queries and updates directly against databases, bypassing application layers where invariants reside. Such code may be generated on demand and discarded afterwards, making the database the only durable component that can encode and enforce these invariants. Second, natural constraints in higher-level conceptual models, such as E/R and property graphs, become fragmented across relations under mappings chosen for performance. The resulting multi-relation constraints lack direct database support, and only some can be efficiently enforced using existing mechanisms such as triggers. These developments motivate an overhaul of how constraints are defined, mined, managed, and enforced in data management systems. As a first concrete step, we introduce constraint indexes, which represent constraints spanning multiple relations as transactional access paths, and implement a proof of concept as a PostgreSQL extension. Constraint indexes enforce constraints arising from distributed inheritance hierarchies, folded relationships, and folded weak entities, as well as cardinality bounds and functional dependencies, at low overhead relative to no enforcement. Across these workloads, they outperform the better of the correctness-preserving baselines by up to 2.41 times. We also show that LLM-driven writers frequently violate unenforced constraints and behave erratically when provided with a list of constraints to enforce. We close by discussing a few research challenges raised by this agenda.

To achieve this, we first assemble the Join, a large collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks. We pretrain with long contexts of up to 8,192 database cells, using in-context examples from a novel lightweight random-walk retriever. Finally, we leverage context tuning and ensembling to scale up test-time compute. On in-context regression tasks from RelBench, RT-J requires 10x fewer examples on average to match strong feature engineering pipelines with LLM-agent or RDBLearn featurizers and TabICLv2 or LightGBM predictors. Overall, our work pushes the frontier for context-efficient predictions on relational data and highlights the importance of real-world semantics, context engineering and large-scale pretraining for RFMs.

AgentOnto substantially outperforms representative methods, while module-level evaluations confirm the effectiveness of ontology construction, analysis, and updating. These results demonstrate that explicitly constructing, using, and updating enterprise knowledge supports reliable and adaptable data analysis.

papers.title: Joining Large String Collections with Jaro-Winkler Similarity

Existing algorithms for computing the Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings are either slow for short strings or require quadratic time and fail to scale to long strings. To reduce the number of string comparisons, state-of-the-art techniques perform an index-nested-loop join on trie-based indexes; however, they have only been evaluated on small datasets and high similarity thresholds. For lower similarity thresholds that are relevant in practice, these techniques incur an excessive number of costly Jaro-Winkler computations. We present a novel approach for efficient Jaro-Winkler similarity joins on large string collections. Our solution is based on three key techniques: (1) JUMP is a fast algorithm for computing the Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings that runs in linear time for bounded alphabets. (2) Dual-bound intersection bitmaps encode strings -- represented as character sets -- into fixed-size bitmaps, which are used to prune candidate string pairs by providing effective bounds on their character overlap; unlike prior bitmap techniques, our bitmaps are equipped with a cost model and adapt to the input data. (3) Our PUMA framework groups strings by prefix to tighten filter conditions, thereby reducing the number of similarity computations. Extensive experiments on large string collections demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms the state of the art, achieving speedups of up to three orders of magnitude.

papers.title: Enumerating Small Potential Maximal Cliques with Fixed-Parameter Delay

papers.abstract: A potential maximal clique (PMC) of a graph $G$ is a nonempty vertex set that forms a maximal clique in some minimal triangulation of $G$. Listing the PMCs of a graph is a key step in exact algorithms for computing treewidth, minimum fill-in, and related graph parameters. We present a deterministic algorithm that enumerates all PMCs of cardinality at most $k$ in an $n$-vertex graph $G$, without repetition, with delay $2^{O(k^3)}n^4\log n$. This bound also covers the preprocessing time before the first output, the time from the last output to termination, and the total running time when no such PMC exists. At the core of our enumeration algorithm is a procedure that solves the following constrained search problem within the same time bound: given sets of required and excluded vertices $I,O\subseteq V(G)$, find a PMC $Ω$ of size at most $k$ satisfying $I\subseteqΩ$ and $Ω\cap O=\emptyset$, or determine that none exists. Our enumeration algorithm directly supports these inclusion and exclusion constraints as well. Our approach builds on the \emph{recursive understanding} technique of Chitnis et al.~\cite{chitnis2016} and the reduction to unbreakable graphs of Lokshtanov et al.~\cite{lokshtanov2018}. A graph is $(q,k)$-unbreakable if no removal of at most $k$ vertices leaves two disjoint unions of connected components that each contain more than $q$ vertices. We first solve constrained PMC search on $(q,k)$-unbreakable graphs, and then apply this procedure to replace separated subgraphs with graphs of size $2^{O(k^2)}$ that preserve the existence of a constrained solution for every graph attached along the shared boundary.

papers.title: Data.Readme: Documenting Table Relationships for Diverse Data Tasks

We present Data.Readme, a novel table documentation approach that uses lightweight offline processing to infer and index rich \emph{table-to-table relationships}, including confusable, joinable, and union-able tables. We further develop a suite of agentic tools for LLMs to work with the index, to help agents retrieve relevant tables and perform tasks much more efficiently and effectively. Finally, we study how to optimize our index construction with a budget constraint. On data lakes containing up to 12K tables, Data.Readme improves task accuracy by as much as 40 percentage points across a range of data discovery, data analysis, and data science tasks, outperforming diverse baselines, including powerful coding agents with unlimited time and monetary budgets. We also show that equipping existing methods (such as coding agents) with Data.Readme can not only lead to consistent quality gains, but also significantly reduce their latency by up to 6x, demonstrating the potential of Data.Readme.

papers.title: Uber-Join: Unifying Diverse Table Joins using LLMs with Precision and Cost Guarantees
papers.importance_reason: 带基准测试，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: When two tables from different sources are joined, the values that should join often differ in spelling, format, or meaning, and fuzzy-, transformation-, and semantic-joins each handle one type of these differences. Large language models (LLMs) can match values that differ in several ways at once, but every LLM call is billed, and having an LLM compare the rows of two large tables can cost far more than a typical budget allows. This paper studies how to combine these join types with LLMs to join two tables under a dollar budget, maximizing recall while keeping the precision of the result at or above a target, a problem that is NP-hard. Our key idea is to use LLMs selectively to create join programs and verify their outputs through sampling, while adaptively deciding which joins to pursue under budget and precision constraints. This combines the scalability of program-based joins with selective LLM verification, while maintaining a statistical precision guarantee on the accumulated result. We develop Uber-Join, which treats creating a join and checking the output of a created join as two levels of arms in a budgeted multi-armed bandit. It commits an output only if the precision of the whole result, estimated from an LLM's judgments of sampled pairs, stays at or above the target with high confidence. Under the same budget, Uber-Join achieves the highest recall at the precision target in nearly all settings on three join benchmarks and Join-Hard, a new benchmark of large tables.

papers.title: Towards Training and Inference of Graph Neural Networks in Graph Databases
papers.importance_reason: 贴近真实场景
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks on large graphs commonly rely on in-memory graph storage with ad hoc data processing pipelines for both training and inference. Graph databases provide scalable storage and efficient traversal for graphs that can evolve over time, but their applicability in GNN training and inference are rarely studied. We show that graph DBs can be used in GNN training and inference directly, executing sampling, feature retrieval, and even the full forward pass. We show different GNN training pipelines can perform on-the-fly sampling and retrieval in graph DBs using Cypher. We further provide optimisations that speed up the training process by \~2.5x while maintaining the same accuracy. We illustrate that fully in-DB inference is possible, independent of how the GNNs are trained. Our inference setup can be >10x faster than cold loading the graph into RAM with no extra memory overhead on real-world graphs. Our work lays the foundation for in-graph-DB GNN training and inference.

papers.title: FAOPs: Normal Forms and an Algebra for AI Agent Workflows
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly encode operational procedures as multi-step agent skills, here called Agent Operating Procedures (AOPs), that must be traceable, auditable, reproducible, access-controlled, and bounded in time and cost, requirements that regulated sectors make mandatory. Yet AOPs are typically kept as coarse-grained files, in which steps bundle actions, copied procedures drift apart, any step may reach any tool, and refactoring goes unchecked. We present Functional Agent Operating Procedures (FAOP), a formal theory that brings database-grade discipline to AI agent workflows. FAOP recasts each workflow as a typed function over scoped state and subjects an entire library to four progressive normal forms: Decomposed (FNF-1) splits a workflow into atomic steps, Typed (FNF-2) makes its data flow explicit and type-checked, Factored (FNF-3) gives each shared procedure a single canonical definition so a change propagates instead of drifting, and Scoped (FNF-4) confines every step to least-privilege tool access. Once normalized, every atomic step is a separate entity with a declared contract and can be type-checked, scope-confined, bounded, tested, traced, and audited on its own. A FAOP algebra of provably sound equalities turns refactoring and parallelization into compiler rewrites; orthogonal extensions add verified termination (+V), optimization (+O), and time and cost bounds (+B); and an architectural-level classifier (0-3) determines whether a workflow needs AI at all. Together, these make integrity, isolation, typing, termination, cost, and optimization compile-time concerns across the whole library, not runtime hopes. We implement the theory in SkillBase, an AOP management system (what PostgreSQL is to data, SkillBase is to AOPs), together with a separate executor that enforces these guarantees at run time. A worked financial workflow illustrates the approach end to end.

papers.title: SARP: An On-SSD Index for KVCache with Fast Prefix Matching and Recovery
papers.importance_reason: 关注吞吐
papers.abstract: Distributed LLM serving relies on a global index to locate reusable key-value cache (KVCache) blocks through prefix matching. Losing the index after a crash or restart forces affected requests to recompute existing KVCache on GPUs. Persisting the index restores access after a failure. Existing persistent indexes face a tension between prefix-matching performance and recovery time. A snapshot-backed in-memory index supports fast prefix matching, but rebuilding the full index delays recovery. An on-SSD index avoids this rebuild, but adds storage accesses to prefix matching. Our core insight is that extending a matched prefix over a short span typically requires distinguishing only a few token sequences, suggesting that sparse in-memory routing state may suffice. Prefix matching also accesses block metadata in sequence order, allowing metadata for consecutive blocks to be retrieved together. We present SARP (Sparse Adaptive Routing and Packing), an on-SSD KVCache index for fast recovery and prefix matching. SARP groups consecutive block IDs and metadata into segments to amortize storage accesses across multiple blocks. A compact in-memory routing directory identifies candidate segments using entries at selected block positions. SARP limits segment retrievals and uses compact filters to prioritize candidates with longer potential matches. After retrieval, SARP verifies block IDs against the query and reuses only KVCache blocks covered by the verified prefix. After a restart, SARP restores the sparse routing directory from a snapshot. Across four multi-turn chat and agentic workloads, SARP recovers 8.0x to 77.5x faster than the in-memory index baselines and delivers 1.15x to 66.6x the request throughput of the on-SSD index baselines, while reusing only 0.0030% to 0.029% fewer tokens than exact prefix matching.

papers.title: SWatcher+: A Holistic Approach to Deploying Learned Cardinality Estimators in a Dynamic Setting
papers.importance_reason: 涉及基数估计
papers.abstract: Cardinality estimation (CE) is crucial in database query optimization. Although recent advances have improved accuracy, deploying machine-learned CE models in dynamic databases remains challenging due to data updates and workload shifts. Retraining can be costly, but existing practices offer little guidance on when and how to update models, resulting in simple periodic retaining strategies that are suboptimal. We propose SWatcher+, a framework that adapts learned CE to dynamic workloads by monitoring data updates and query feedback. SWatcher+ selectively monitors high-impact subqueries for which wrong estimates lead to poor plan performance, and it proactively applies corrections to estimates during query optimization. This strategy enables immediate adaption to data and workload shifts without waiting for full model retraining, and carefully balances the cost and benefit of monitoring and adaption versus retraining. Our experiments show that SWatcher+ offers a better trade-off between query performance and overhead compared with existing approaches, making it a more practical solution for deploying learned CE in dynamic settings.

papers.title: Contestable Agents for Data Governance: Recording Human Stewardship of AI-Generated Metadata Across Structured and Unstructured Systems
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: Industrial organizations hold operational knowledge in structured records, such as telemetry, point lists, and transactions, and in unstructured sources, such as manuals, service notes, communications, and inspection reports. Governance programs often manage these sources separately. Classifying, linking, and documenting them depends on a small group of employees with deep domain knowledge. Agents built on large language models can propose metadata, cite documents, and flag quality issues, but unreviewed proposals can spread errors into downstream systems. A perfunctory approval leaves no record of what a reviewer checked. We present contestable governance: specialist agents produce scored, cited arguments for disputed metadata decisions; a steward can accept, reject, modify, or add arguments before commit; and a governance record retains the evidence, interventions, and outcome. A versioned domain glossary supplies model-specific terms and acronym definitions to the agents. We describe the workflow, a triage path that reserves full argumentation for uncertain proposals while preserving review before commit, the scoring and record models, and a gate that controls which verified decisions become precedent. Two HVAC use cases illustrate the pattern: point classification using Brick Schema class labels, supported by an open reference implementation, and an illustrative warranty failure-mode decision linking claim fields and telemetry to service notes and revisioned bulletins.

papers.title: Data Provenance Aggregation and Structural Descriptors for Query-Template Identification
papers.importance_reason: 有实验评估
papers.abstract: Runtime query similarity identification supports several activities, including workload analysis, identifying recurring behaviour, auditing, debugging, and anomaly detection. Existing methods for evaluating query similarity mostly rely on SQL text, execution plans, or result values but do not account for input data or how results are derived during query execution. This paper proposes a novel approach using data provenance for query-template identification. We construct query-level profiles that capture explicit data dependencies, occurrence frequencies, and structural properties by aggregating tuple-level Lineage and Why-provenance across entire query results. We also derive Provenance Structural Descriptors (PSD), which summarise these profiles using a small set of numerical features. We evaluate our proposals using these profiles to identify query templates over \(12{,}500\) distinct query instances generated from parametrised TPC-DS query templates. The experimental evaluation shows that query templates can be identified solely from their provenance footprints, and that accuracy improves as more historical data becomes available. It also shows that PSD achieve high classification accuracy with limited training history and low test-processing cost.

papers.title: Containment of Conjunctive Queries with Negative Information over Semirings
papers.importance_reason: 涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: We study the containment problem for (unions of) conjunctive queries ((U)CQs) with negative information on semiring-annotated databases. Our approach to negative information follows the treatment of negation proposed by Grädel and Tannen (2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024) for first-order logic and fixed point logic which applies productively to large classes of semirings, including bounded distributive lattices, as well as the important provenance semirings studied for positive CQ containment by Green (2009). Negation features in (U)CQs along two dimensions: negated equalities (disequations), and negated relational atoms. We study complexity for each of them separately, as well as jointly. For disequations, we extend a methodology that proves the same complexity bounds as the ones already known for the standard Boolean semiring (in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy) for most semirings of interest. Two prominent exceptions are $\mathbb{N}[X]$ and Trio(X) where the complexity bound for containment is in the second level of the counting hierarchy. For CQs with negated relational atoms we show that the complexity, surprisingly, is the same as that of the containment of CQs without negation when one considers model-defining and provenance-tracking interpretations (namely, nondeterministic polynomial time). Interestingly, among bounded distributive lattices, the Boolean two-element case is the only one where the complexity of the problem continues to be hard for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy for model-defining interpretations. Furthermore, we show that the complexity increases again for distributive lattices if we focus on other classes of interpretations. Finally, we consider queries that have both negated equalities and negated relational atoms and show that the complexity of containment continues to be that of the case with just negated equalities.
